article_title: Rust Language Team Opens Nightly Experiment Testing Function Overloading for C++ Interop

content_preview.title: Rust Language Team Opens Nightly Experiment Testing Function Overloading for C++ Interop
content_preview.summary: Rust's Language Team invited developers to test an experimental nightly feature that lets overloaded FFI functions be called without tuple workarounds.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The Rust Language Team published a call for experimentation on August 19, 2026, inviting compiler and interop tool developers to try a new nightly-only mechanism for calling overloaded functions, according to [Inside Rust](https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/08/19/overloading-experiment/). The work is being carried out "in partnership with the Rust Foundation's Rust-C++ Interop Initiative," which has been "experimenting with function overloading for FFI bindings," the post s...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (572 words, within the 400-1200 News range) using the standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know format. Technical claims about the #[rustc_splat] attribute, the hypot() FFI example, and the tuple-vs-splat calling syntax are explained clearly and accurately for a developer audience without editorializing.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read both source snapshots from disk in full (gunzip'd, no re-WebFetch needed): source-0.html.gz (blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust, sha256 4acbc9236fac84be2e79057deb85b291f293591cc54239da2cda0e8ab58dce6b, matches manifest) and source-1.html.gz (rustfoundation.org, sha256 8a54b583d55c690671cf8fd378810f7149c98949761d3cf6bd6c8b7e6f33912b, matches manifest). Both returned HTTP 200 on the original fetch and manifest.suspicious_patterns is null for both entries -- no regex flags to review. Every direct quote in the article body was checked against the raw extracted snapshot text and appears verbatim, including: '#[rustc_splat] attribute', 'from 2026-07-31 onwards have experimental support for more ergonomic function and method overloading', 'no double parentheses required', 'like most Rust language experiments, this nightly feature has no RFC, and can change or be removed at any time', 'Ajay Singh, a Rust Project Outreachy intern, is working on a macro to make splat-based overloading more ergonomic', 'found a bug or limitation' / '#t-lang/interop channel on Zulip' (Inside Rust); and 'the initiative is funded by Rust Foundation Platinum Member Google, which makes my work as a contractor for the Interop Initiative possible', 'a mapping exercise, not a feature proposal', 'see how far Rust's existing trait system can be pushed to enable foreign-language overload resolution', 'it's not coming to stable Rust any time soon, and it may never ship in anything resembling its current form', 'calling overloaded C++ functions from Rust means writing (or generating) manual boilerplate for every overload, using Rust traits, or creating uniquely named functions for each overload', 'call overloaded FFI functions without thinking about tuples or traits at all', 'just one piece of the broader Rust/C++ Interop Initiative', 'expect another update on the initiative's progress in the coming weeks' (Rust Foundation). Specifically verified per the reviewer brief: (1) the '#[rustc_splat] attribute' name appears verbatim in source-0's code example and prose; (2) the 'nightly-only experimental' status is explicit in both sources ('nightly Rust language experiment', 'no RFC, and can change or be removed at any time' on Inside Rust; 'nightly-only, feature-gated experiment with no RFC' on Rust Foundation); (3) the Google-funded Rust Foundation 'Rust-C++ Interop Initiative' framing traces verbatim to source-0 ('In partnership with the Rust Foundation's Rust-C++ Interop Initiative') and source-1 ('The Rust/C++ Interop Initiative... is funded by Rust Foundation Platinum Member Google'); the two publications use slightly different punctuation for the initiative's name (hyphen on blog.rust-lang.org, slash on rustfoundation.org) but this variance exists in the real sources themselves, not introduced by the bot -- the article's own usage ('Rust-C++ Interop Initiative') matches its Inside Rust citation exactly. (4) Same-day/same-author claim confirmed: source-0 bylines 'Aug. 19, 2026 - teor on behalf of The Language Team'; source-1 bylines 'August 19, 2026 / Teor' and opens 'Today, the Inside Rust blog published a technical write-up I submitted about a new nightly experiment called splat' -- both posts are dated August 19, 2026 and the Rust Foundation post is explicitly authored by the same person (Teor) who wrote the Inside Rust announcement. No misattribution, no hallucinated quotes, no unsupported specifics found.
